opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing that's changed over the past year is that RL in language models has finally been shown to really work. We now have proof that if you give these models the right feedback loop, they can reach expert-level performance on tasks where you have a clean, verifiable reward signal: competitive programming and math are the obvious examples. That was not obvious a couple of years ago. There was a real question about whether RL on top of pre-trained models would just be a thin layer of polish or whether it could actually teach new capabilities, and I think the evidence now points pretty clearly toward the latter.

The caveat is that this works best where you can verify outcomes. Does the code pass the unit tests? Is the answer to the math problem correct? Those domains have moved incredibly fast. Where it's been slower is in long-horizon, messier tasks, things like acting as an agent in a real software engineering environment over many hours, or tasks where "good" is fuzzy and hard to score. The models are getting much better at those too, but the bottleneck there is less about the algorithm and more about building the environments, the feedback signals, and the ability to stay coherent over long contexts.

So my overall read is that the algorithmic question has been largely answered. RL works, and it compounds with pre-training rather than replacing it. The open frontier now is engineering and scaling: richer environments, better reward signals for non-verifiable domains, and extending the horizon over which these models can act reliably. If those pieces come together, I think the next year looks even more dramatic than the last one, especially for agentic software engineering, which I'd expect to be the first domain where you see these systems doing genuinely substantial chunks of real work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it worked, and it worked more cleanly than most of us expected. If you'd asked me eighteen months ago, I would have said RL on language models is promising but fragile. You had to get the reward just right, the models would find weird exploits, and it was hard to tell whether you were actually teaching the model something or just teaching it to pattern-match the grader. What changed is that we found domains where the reward is genuinely verifiable, so math with a checkable answer, code with tests that actually run, and once you have that, the model can do a lot of the learning on its own. You give it a problem, it tries, it gets a signal, it tries again, and you let that loop run for a very long time.

The thing that I think people underrate is how much of the progress came from scale on the RL side specifically, not just the pretraining side. For a long time, RL was this thin layer of polish on top of a massive pretrained model, a tiny fraction of the compute. Over the past year that ratio has shifted meaningfully. Labs are now spending a serious chunk of their total budget on the RL phase, and the capabilities you get from that are qualitatively different. The model isn't just more pleasant to talk to, it can sustain a line of reasoning over thousands of tokens, notice when it's wrong, back up, and try something else. That behavior wasn't really explicitly programmed. It emerged because it was useful for getting the reward.

The caveat I'd give is that most of this has happened in domains where verification is cheap. Math, competitive programming, certain kinds of agentic tasks where you can check if the thing got done. The open question, and the thing I spend most of my time thinking about, is how far that transfers. Does getting really good at verifiable reasoning make the model better at writing a thoughtful essay or making a judgment call where there's no clean answer? My read is that it transfers more than the skeptics thought and less than the optimists hoped. The models are clearly smarter in a general sense, but you can still see the seams where the training signal was strong versus where it was weak.

The other thing I'd flag is that we've basically confirmed the models can learn from the environments we give them, which means the bottleneck has shifted. It's less about the algorithm now and more about building good environments, rich tasks, realistic tools, long horizons where the model has to actually plan. That's an engineering problem more than a research problem, which in some ways is reassuring, because engineering problems tend to get solved. But it also means the pace isn't going to slow down just because we've run out of clever ideas. The clever idea works. Now it's about feeding it.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that reinforcement learning has started to look like a way of teaching models to solve problems, rather than just a way of making their answers more pleasant to read.

With preference training, you’re often rewarding an answer that looks good to a human evaluator. But if you have a task where you can check the result—does the code pass the tests, did you get the math problem right—you can reward success directly. That gives the model room to discover approaches that you didn’t explicitly demonstrate.

The interesting question is how far that generalizes. Getting better at problems with clean, verifiable answers is valuable, but a lot of useful work has much messier feedback. Did you do good research? Did you make the right engineering tradeoff? Those are harder things to turn into a reward signal.

So I’d distinguish two claims. One is that RL can substantially improve a language model’s ability to reason through a problem. I think the evidence for that has become much stronger. The other is that we’ve figured out how to apply it to the full range of tasks we care about. That’s still an open question, and probably where a lot of the most interesting work is.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the progress has been pretty striking, especially in domains where you can reliably check whether an answer is right. Coding and math are the obvious examples. A pretrained model already has a lot of relevant knowledge, but reinforcement learning can make it much better at using that knowledge: spending longer on a problem, checking an approach, noticing a mistake, and trying something else.

The harder question is how broadly that transfers. If you can run the code or verify the mathematical answer, you have a fairly clean training signal. For something like doing research, you might not know whether a decision was good until much later. And if your reward is only an imperfect proxy for what you want, optimizing it harder can expose those imperfections.

So I’d distinguish between ‘RL is producing substantial capability gains,’ which I think is pretty clear, and ‘we know how to apply it to every economically useful task,’ which is a much stronger claim. What’s exciting is that we now have a productive way to improve reasoning after pretraining. How far that goes as we improve the tasks, the feedback, and the amount of training is still an open question.
